content: Vitamin D deficiency is a widespread issue globally, and its prevalence has been increasing in recent years. In the United States, vitamin D deficiency is more common among non-white ethnic groups. The prevalence of deficiency varies depending on the laboratory methods used and the threshold set for defining deficiency. For example, 8% of the U.S. population has serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD) levels below 40 nmol/L. Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (NHANES) conducted between 2001 and 2006 indicate that one-quarter of the population was at risk of vitamin D inadequacy (serum 25OHD levels between 30–49 nmol/L), and 8% were at risk of vitamin D deficiency (serum 25OHD levels below 30 nmol/L). In Canada, statistics from the Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) Cycle 1 (2007–2009) show that 13% of Canadians have vitamin D levels below 40 nmol/L. A study by Naugler et al. using data from Calgary Laboratory Services and Census Canada (2010–2011) found that 26% of individuals over the age of 25 in Calgary, Alberta, had serum 25OHD levels below 50 nmol/L. Age In both males and females, the prevalence of vitamin D deficiency is lowest in children aged 1–8 years. The risk of deficiency increases significantly with age, peaking at age 30 in males and age 18 in females, after which it does not change significantly with age. Gender Vitamin D deficiency is slightly more prevalent in females than in males. According to NHANES data from 2001–2006, the season-adjusted prevalence of deficiency risk ranged from 1% to 8% in males and 1% to 12% in females, depending on age. Race Non-Hispanic white individuals are at a lower risk of vitamin D deficiency compared to African Americans, Hispanics, and Asians. A study by Gozdzik et al. on 107 young adults in Toronto during the winter of 2007 demonstrated an association between serum 25OHD levels and skin pigmentation. Developed Countries In developed countries, the prevalence of severe vitamin D deficiency (serum 25OHD levels <25 nmol/L) is 15% in the United States and 4% in Europe, as reported by Chowdhury et al. In the Uppsala Longitudinal Study of Adult Men, a cohort study of 1,194 Swedish men during the winter season, only 5% had serum 25OHD levels below 40 nmol/L. Developing Countries In developing countries, vitamin D deficiency is also highly prevalent. A study by Puri et al. on 3,127 schoolgirls in Delhi found that 88% had insufficient serum 25OHD levels (<50 nmol/L), regardless of socioeconomic status. Vitamin D deficiency is particularly common among Saudi women, with approximately 80% of women in a study by Adarawi et al. showing serum 25OHD levels below 50 nmol/L. In contrast, Thailand has relatively higher serum 25OHD levels compared to European, Middle Eastern, and other Asian countries. A study by Chailurkit et al. reported a 3% prevalence of vitamin D deficiency (<50 nmol/L) across different regions of Thailand.
